_note: Comparison data for Milnor §§20–24 (Exposition chapters 12–15). The items V15.x (§24) follow the V14 block, and their notFormalized entries follow those of §§20–23 (the G-numbering follows file order).

items.title: The algebraic model of a bi-invariant metric

milnor.label: §21, p. 113
milnor.statement: Milnor works with the Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant vector fields on a Lie group $G$ with a left and right invariant metric, the bracket of vector fields, and the connection $X \vdash Y$ of the metric; Theorem 21.3 (a) is the identity $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle = \langle X, [Y, Z]\rangle$.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): $B$ is ad-invariant if $B([X, Y], Z) = B(X, [Y, Z])$ for all $X, Y, Z$, which is Mathlib's Lie invariance. A bilinear $D : L \times L \to L$, standing for $X \vdash Y$, is Levi-Civita for $B$ if $D(X, Y) - D(Y, X) = [X, Y]$ and $B(D(X, Y), Z) + B(Y, D(X, Z)) = 0$.

chips: an abstract Lie algebra with a form
diff: The group, its left-invariant fields and its metric are replaced by an abstract Lie algebra with a bilinear form. That $X \vdash Y$ is again left-invariant, which Milnor uses without comment when he applies (d) twice, is built into the definition. For matrix groups the model is derived from the geometry (V12.17).

items.title: Theorem 21.3 (d): $X \vdash Y = \frac12[X, Y]$

milnor.label: §21, proof of Theorem 21.3, pp. 113–114
milnor.statement: In the proof of Theorem 21.3: the integral curves of a left-invariant $X$ are left translates of one-parameter subgroups, hence geodesics, so $X \vdash X = 0$; expanding $(X + Y) \vdash (X + Y) = 0$ and adding $X \vdash Y - Y \vdash X = [X, Y]$ gives (d), $X \vdash Y = \frac12[X, Y]$.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): if $D$ is Levi-Civita for $B$ (no condition on $B$) and $D(X, X) = 0$ for every $X$, then $D(X, Y) = \frac12[X, Y]$ for all $X, Y$.

diff: $X \vdash X = 0$ rests on Lemma 21.2 and on left translations being isometries; here it is a hypothesis. For matrix groups it is proved (V12.15, V12.17).

items.title: Theorem 21.3 (a): the metric is ad-invariant

milnor.label: §21, Theorem 21.3 (a)
milnor.statement: Let $G$ have a bi-invariant metric and $X, Y, Z \in \mathfrak g$. Then $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle = \langle X, [Y, Z]\rangle$. Proof (p. 114): $Y\langle X, Z\rangle = \langle Y \vdash X, Z\rangle + \langle X, Y \vdash Z\rangle$, the left side vanishes since $\langle X, Z\rangle$ is constant, and (d) is substituted.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): if $D$ is Levi-Civita for $B$ and $D(X, X) = 0$ for every $X$, then $B$ is ad-invariant.

diff: The constancy of $\langle X, Z\rangle$ for left-invariant fields is built into the compatibility condition of V12.1, and $X \vdash X = 0$ is a hypothesis.

items.title: The Koszul formula: the connection is forced to be $\frac12[\,,\,]$

milnor.label: §21, cf. Theorem 21.3, p. 113
milnor.statement: The book has no such statement. Milnor derives (d) from $X \vdash X = 0$; that the Levi-Civita connection of a bi-invariant metric must be $\frac12[\,,\,]$ on left-invariant fields is the uniqueness of Lemma 8.6 in this setting.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): if $B$ is symmetric and $D$ Levi-Civita for $B$, then $2B(D(X, Y), Z) = B([X, Y], Z) - B([Y, Z], X) + B([Z, X], Y)$; if moreover $B$ is ad-invariant and non-degenerate, $D(X, Y) = \frac12[X, Y]$. Conversely, for every ad-invariant $B$, $\frac12[\,,\,]$ is Levi-Civita for $B$.

diff: Derives (d) from the ad-invariance of the metric instead of from $X \vdash X = 0$.

items.title: Theorem 21.3 (b): $R(X, Y)Z = \frac14[[X, Y], Z]$

milnor.label: §21, Theorem 21.3 (b)
milnor.statement: Let $G$ have a bi-invariant metric and $X, Y, Z \in \mathfrak g$. Then $R(X, Y)Z = \frac14[[X, Y], Z]$. Proof (p. 114): substitute (d) in $R(X, Y)Z = -X \vdash (Y \vdash Z) + Y \vdash (X \vdash Z) + [X, Y] \vdash Z$ and use the Jacobi identity.

lean.statement: In any real Lie algebra, with Milnor's sign $R(X, Y)Z = -D(X, D(Y, Z)) + D(Y, D(X, Z)) + D([X, Y], Z)$ and $D = \frac12[\,,\,]$: $R(X, Y)Z = \frac14[[X, Y], Z]$.

diff: A computation in the Lie algebra; that it is the curvature of the group is V12.17 for matrix groups.

items.title: Theorem 21.3 (c)

milnor.label: §21, Theorem 21.3 (c)
milnor.statement: $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [Z, W]\rangle$; it "follows from (a) and (b)" (p. 114).

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): if $B$ is ad-invariant, then $B(R(X, Y)Z, W) = \frac14B([X, Y], [Z, W])$ for $D = \frac12[\,,\,]$.

diff: As in V12.5.

items.title: Cartan's 3-form

milnor.label: §21, footnote, p. 114
milnor.statement: The trilinear function $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle$ is skew-symmetric in all three variables, so it defines a left-invariant 3-form; Cartan used it to prove $H^3(G) \neq 0$ for a compact connected non-abelian Lie group.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): $B([Y, X], Z) = -B([X, Y], Z)$ for every $B$, and $B([X, Z], Y) = -B([X, Y], Z)$ if $B$ is ad-invariant; so $(X, Y, Z) \mapsto B([X, Y], Z)$ is alternating.

diff: The differential form, its de Rham class and Cartan's theorem are not formalized.

items.title: Corollary 21.4: the sectional curvature

milnor.label: §21, Corollary 21.4
milnor.statement: The sectional curvature $\langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [X, Y]\rangle$ is always $\ge 0$, with equality iff $[X, Y] = 0$.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): if $B$ is ad-invariant, $B(R(X, Y)X, Y) = \frac14B([X, Y], [X, Y])$ for all $X, Y$; if $B$ is also positive definite this is $\ge 0$, and $0$ iff $[X, Y] = 0$. With the standard sign, $B(-R(X, Y)Y, X) = \frac14B([X, Y], [X, Y])$.

chips: for all $X, Y$, not only orthonormal pairs

items.title: Corollary 21.5, the algebraic step: positive Ricci curvature

milnor.label: §21, Corollary 21.5
milnor.statement: If the Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of a Lie group $G$ with a bi-invariant metric has trivial centre, then $G$ is compact with finite fundamental group. Proof: the Ricci curvature $K(X_1, X_1) = \sum_i\langle R(X_1, X_i)X_1, X_i\rangle$ is strictly positive and bounded away from zero, and Myers' theorem (Corollary 19.5) applies.

lean.statement: Let $K_V = -\frac14\operatorname{ad}_V^2$, so that $K_V(W) = R(V, W)V$ for $D = \frac12[\,,\,]$. In every real Lie algebra $\operatorname{tr}K_V = -\frac14\kappa(V, V)$, $\kappa$ the Killing form. If $L$ is finite-dimensional, $B$ symmetric, positive definite and ad-invariant and the centre of $L$ is $0$, then $\operatorname{tr}K_V > 0$ for $V \neq 0$; equivalently $\kappa$ is negative definite.

chips: only the positivity of the Ricci curvature
diff: The uniform bound, Myers' theorem for $G$, compactness and the finiteness of $\pi_1$ are not formalized. Milnor omits "connected", which cannot be dropped ($SO(3) \times \mathbb Z$).

items.title: Corollary 21.6, the algebraic step: splitting off the centre

milnor.label: §21, Corollary 21.6
milnor.statement: A simply connected Lie group $G$ with a bi-invariant metric splits as $G' \times \mathbb R^k$, $G'$ compact with Lie algebra of trivial centre. Proof (pp. 115–116): the orthogonal complement $\mathfrak g'$ of the centre $\mathfrak c$ is a subalgebra, since $\langle[X, Y], C\rangle = \langle X, [Y, C]\rangle = 0$, and $\mathfrak g = \mathfrak g' \oplus \mathfrak c$.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$): for ad-invariant $B$, $\mathfrak g' = \{X : B(C, X) = 0 \text{ for } C \in \mathfrak c\}$ is a Lie ideal; if $L$ is finite-dimensional and $B$ symmetric, positive definite and ad-invariant, $L = \mathfrak c \oplus \mathfrak g'$ and $\mathfrak g'$ has trivial centre.

chips: an ideal, not only a subalgebra
diff: The splitting of the simply connected group and the compactness of $G'$ are not formalized. $\mathfrak g'$ is shown to be an ideal, which is what the splitting uses.

items.title: The operator $K_V$ in the proof of Theorem 21.7

milnor.label: §21, proof of Theorem 21.7, pp. 116–117
milnor.statement: $K_V(W) = R(V, W)V = \frac14[[V, W], V]$, so $K_V = -\frac14(\operatorname{Ad}V)\circ(\operatorname{Ad}V)$, and $\operatorname{Ad}V$ is skew-symmetric by 21.3 (a).

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$) ad-invariant: $\operatorname{ad}_V$ is skew, $K_V$ is self-adjoint and $B(K_VW, W) = \frac14B([V, W], [V, W])$. If $B$ is also positive definite, $K_V$ is positive semi-definite, $K_VW = 0$ iff $[V, W] = 0$, every eigenvalue of $K_V$ is $\ge 0$, and the only real eigenvalue of $\operatorname{ad}_V$ is $0$.

chips: the kernel of $K_V$ is the centralizer

items.title: The non-zero eigenvalues of $K_V$ occur in pairs

milnor.label: §21, proof of Theorem 21.7, p. 117
milnor.statement: Choosing an orthonormal basis that puts $\operatorname{Ad}V$ in block form with blocks $\begin{pmatrix}0 & a_i\\ -a_i & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $(\operatorname{Ad}V)^2$ is diagonal with entries $-a_1^2, -a_1^2, -a_2^2, \dots$; so the non-zero eigenvalues of $K_V$ are positive and occur in pairs.

lean.statement: For a real Lie algebra $L$ (standing for Milnor's $\mathfrak g$ of left-invariant fields) with a bilinear form $B$ (his inner product on $\mathfrak g$) ad-invariant and positive definite, $L$ finite-dimensional: $K_VW = \mu W$ iff $[V, [V, W]] = -4\mu W$; $\operatorname{ad}_V$ preserves each eigenspace $E_\mu$; for $\mu > 0$, $J = (2\sqrt\mu)^{-1}\operatorname{ad}_V$ satisfies $J^2 = -1$ on $E_\mu$ and preserves $B$; so every eigenspace of $K_V$ for $\mu \neq 0$ has even dimension.

chips: a complex structure, not the normal form
diff: The normal form of a skew-symmetric map, quoted without proof, is replaced by the complex structure $J$ on each eigenspace, which is what "occur in pairs" needs.

items.title: Even index from paired eigenvalues

milnor.label: §21, proof of Theorem 21.7, p. 117
milnor.statement: By 20.5 the conjugate points occur in pairs, every conjugate point has even multiplicity, and with the Index Theorem the index of every geodesic from $p$ to $q$ is even.

lean.statement: For real numbers $e_1, \dots, e_N$ (a spectrum of $K_V$ with multiplicity), the index of the spectrum is $\sum_{0 < t < 1}\#\{i : e_i > 0,\ t \in \pi\mathbb Z/\sqrt{e_i}\}$ (Theorems 20.5 and 15.1 written as a definition, V14.7–V14.8). If every positive value occurs an even number of times, the index is even.

diff: Theorems 20.5 and 15.1 enter as a definition here; for $SU(n)$ they are proved (V14.18, V14.19). Passing from even-dimensional eigenspaces (V12.12) to even multiplicities in a list needs the spectral theorem for $K_V$, which is not formalized in this form, so Theorem 21.7 is not assembled.

items.title: Matrix groups and their bi-invariant metric

milnor.label: §21, p. 112; §23, p. 125
milnor.statement: A Lie group $G$ with a metric invariant under left and right translations; if $G$ is compact such a metric exists, by averaging any metric with the Haar measure (p. 112). For $U(n)$ the tangent space at $I$ is the space of skew-Hermitian matrices (p. 125, (6)).

lean.statement: Multiplication by a unitary matrix is a linear isometry of $M_n(\mathbb K)$. A matrix group is a slice submanifold $G \subseteq M_n(\mathbb K)$ with a real Lie subalgebra $\mathfrak g$ such that every $g \in G$ is unitary, $G$ is closed under products and adjoints, $\mathfrak g$ consists of skew-Hermitian matrices and is invariant under $X \mapsto gXg^*$, $\exp\mathfrak g \subseteq G$, and $\dim G = \dim\mathfrak g$. Then $T_gG = g\mathfrak g$, left and right translations by elements of $G$ are isometries of $M_n(\mathbb K)$ preserving $G$ (the metric is bi-invariant), and the inner product on $\mathfrak g$ is ad-invariant and positive definite.

diff: Milnor's abstract Lie groups and left-invariant fields are replaced by groups of matrices with the induced metric; every compact Lie group is one (Peter–Weyl), which is not needed for §§23–24. The algebra of V12.1–V12.13 applies to $(\mathfrak g, \langle\,,\rangle)$.

items.title: Lemma 21.2: the geodesics are the one-parameter subgroups

milnor.label: §21, Lemma 21.2
milnor.statement: The geodesics $\gamma$ with $\gamma(0) = e$ are precisely the one-parameter subgroups of $G$. (By Corollary 20.2, p. 110, a symmetric space is complete.)

lean.statement: For a matrix group $(G, \mathfrak g)$ — a slice submanifold $G$ of the space $M_n(\mathbb K)$ of matrices ($\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$), with the induced metric of $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$, and a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of skew-Hermitian matrices (V12.14): $t \mapsto g\exp(tX)$, $g \in G$, $X \in \mathfrak g$, is a geodesic on $\mathbb R$; a geodesic on a preconnected open set $s \ni t_0$ is $\gamma(t_0)\exp((t - t_0)X)$ with $X = \gamma(t_0)^*\gamma'(t_0) \in \mathfrak g$. (i) A geodesic $\gamma : \mathbb R \to G$ with $\gamma(0) = I$ is $t \mapsto \exp(t\gamma'(0))$ and satisfies $\gamma(s + t) = \gamma(s)\gamma(t)$. (ii) A differentiable $\theta : \mathbb R \to G$ with $\theta(0) = I$ and $\theta(s + t) = \theta(s)\theta(t)$ is a geodesic. $\exp_g(gX) = g\exp X$, and $G$ is geodesically complete.

diff: For matrix groups only. Milnor's proof of (i) uses 20.1 and passes from commensurable parameters to all of $\mathbb R$ "by continuity"; here the acceleration $g\exp(tX)X^2$ is normal ($X^2$ is Hermitian), and uniqueness of geodesics gives the converse.

items.title: Lemma 21.1: the reflection $\sigma \mapsto \tau\sigma^{-1}\tau$

milnor.label: §21, Lemma 21.1
milnor.statement: If $G$ has a bi-invariant metric, then for each $\tau$ the map $I_\tau(\sigma) = \tau\sigma^{-1}\tau$ is an isometry which fixes $\tau$ and reverses geodesics through $\tau$; so $G$ is a symmetric space.

lean.statement: For a matrix group $(G, \mathfrak g)$ — a slice submanifold $G$ of the space $M_n(\mathbb K)$ of matrices ($\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$), with the induced metric of $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$, and a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of skew-Hermitian matrices (V12.14): for unitary $\tau$, $A \mapsto \tau A^*\tau$ is an involutive linear isometry of $M_n(\mathbb K)$, equal to $\sigma \mapsto \tau\sigma^{-1}\tau$ on $G$; for $\tau \in G$ it maps $G$ into $G$, fixes $\tau$, and $I_\tau(\tau\exp(tX)) = \tau\exp(-tX)$ for $X \in \mathfrak g$.

diff: By V12.15 the curves $\tau\exp(tX)$ are all the geodesics through $\tau$. A symmetric space is not defined, so the last clause is not a formal statement; it would also need $G$ connected.

items.title: Theorem 21.3 and Corollary 21.4 for matrix groups

milnor.label: §21, Theorem 21.3 and Corollary 21.4
milnor.statement: Let $G$ have a bi-invariant metric and $X, Y, Z, W \in \mathfrak g$. Then (a) $\langle[X, Y], Z\rangle = \langle X, [Y, Z]\rangle$, (b) $R(X, Y)Z = \frac14[[X, Y], Z]$, (c) $\langle R(X, Y)Z, W\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [Z, W]\rangle$; in the proof, (d) $X \vdash Y = \frac12[X, Y]$. Corollary 21.4 (p. 115): $\langle R(X, Y)X, Y\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [X, Y]\rangle \ge 0$.

lean.statement: For a matrix group $(G, \mathfrak g)$ — a slice submanifold $G$ of the space $M_n(\mathbb K)$ of matrices ($\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$), with the induced metric of $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$, and a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of skew-Hermitian matrices (V12.14), $g \in G$, $X, Y, Z, W \in \mathfrak g$: (a) holds; (d) the covariant derivative of $q \mapsto qY$ in the direction $gX$ is $g\cdot\frac12[X, Y]$; the second fundamental form is $\mathrm{II}_g(gX, gY) = \frac12g(XY + YX)$; (b) $R(gX, gY)gZ = \frac14g[[X, Y], Z]$ (Milnor's sign), which is $g$ times the algebraic curvature of V12.5, and $R(gA, gW)gA = g\,K_A(W)$; (c) $\langle R(gX, gY)gZ, gW\rangle = \frac14\langle[X, Y], [Z, W]\rangle$; and $\langle R(gX, gY)gX, gY\rangle = \frac14\|[X, Y]\|^2 \ge 0$, zero iff $XY = YX$.

diff: For matrix groups. (b) is proved by the Gauss equation of the submanifold $G$ (V6.18) and a trace identity, not by substituting (d) into the definition of $R$; this removes, for matrix groups, the hypotheses of V12.1–V12.3.

items.title: Theorem 20.5 for matrix groups: the Jacobi equation along $\exp(tA)$

milnor.label: §20, Theorem 20.5
milnor.statement: Let $\gamma$ be a geodesic in a locally symmetric manifold with $\gamma(0) = p$, $\gamma'(0) = V$, and $e_1, \dots, e_n$ the eigenvalues of $K_V(W) = R(V, W)V$. The conjugate points to $p$ along $\gamma$ are the $\gamma(\pi k/\sqrt{e_i})$, $k$ a non-zero integer, $e_i > 0$; the multiplicity of $\gamma(t)$ is the number of $e_i$ such that $t$ is a multiple of $\pi/\sqrt{e_i}$. Proof (p. 111): in a parallel orthonormal eigenframe the Jacobi equation is $w_i'' + e_iw_i = 0$.

lean.statement: For a matrix group $(G, \mathfrak g)$ — a slice submanifold $G$ of the space $M_n(\mathbb K)$ of matrices ($\mathbb K = \mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$), with the induced metric of $\langle A, B\rangle = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(A^*B)$, and a Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ of skew-Hermitian matrices (V12.14), $A \in \mathfrak g$, $\gamma(t) = \exp(tA)$, $h(t) = \exp(tA/2)$: the covariant derivative of $hUh$ along $\gamma$ is $hU'h$ for $\mathfrak g$-valued $U$, and $R(\gamma', hMh)\gamma' = h\,K_A(M)\,h$ with $K_A(M) = \frac14[[A, M], A]$. Hence if $U$ is smooth with $U'' + K_A(U) = 0$, $hUh$ is a Jacobi field along $\gamma$ with covariant derivative $U'(0)$ at $0$.

diff: Only along one-parameter subgroups of matrix groups, and only the implication from the constant-coefficient equation $U'' + K_A(U) = 0$ to Jacobi fields. The frame $U \mapsto hUh$ replaces the parallel eigenframe. The count of conjugate points with multiplicities is proved for $SU(n)$ (V14.18); locally symmetric spaces are not defined.

items.title: The space $\Omega^d$ of minimal geodesics

milnor.label: §22, p. 118
milnor.statement: $\Omega^d$ denotes the space of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$, where $d = \rho(p, q)^2$ and $M$ is complete.

lean.statement: For a slice submanifold $N$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, with the induced metric, $p, q \in N$ and $\Omega = \Omega(N; p, q)$ with Milnor's metric (V10.1): $\Omega^d$ is the set of paths whose energy is at most that of every path of $\Omega$; a path of least energy is an unbroken geodesic.

diff: By Lemma 12.1 (V8.6) the paths of least energy are the minimal geodesics parametrized proportionally to arc length, and $d = \rho(p, q)^2$; here $d$ is not named.

items.title: Theorem 22.1

milnor.label: §22, Theorem 22.1
milnor.statement: If the space $\Omega^d$ of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$ is a topological manifold, and if every non-minimal geodesic from $p$ to $q$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$, then $\pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0$ for $0 \le i < \lambda_0$. ($M$ is complete throughout §22; proof pp. 122–123.)

lean.statement: For a slice submanifold $N$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, with the induced metric, $p, q \in N$ and $\Omega = \Omega(N; p, q)$ with Milnor's metric (V10.1): let the closed balls about $p$ be compact, let every geodesic of $\Omega$ not of least energy have index $\ge \lambda_0$, and let $\Omega^d$ be a retract of an open neighbourhood in $\Omega$ (an open $O \supseteq \Omega^d$ and $\rho : O \to \Omega^d$, continuous on $O$, the identity on $\Omega^d$). Let $P$ be compact with a continuous injection into a real vector space of dimension $< \lambda_0$ (e.g. $I^i$, $i < \lambda_0$). Then every map $h : P \to \Omega$ is homotopic, relative to $h^{-1}(\Omega^d)$, to a map into $\Omega^d$; equivalently the inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega$ compresses maps from $P$.

diff: The hypothesis "$\Omega^d$ is a topological manifold" is replaced by its consequence that $\Omega^d$ is a retract of an open neighbourhood, which is all the proof uses: Milnor gets it from Hanner's theorem, which is not formalized. For the sphere and for $SU(2m)$ the retraction is constructed (V13.8, V14.21).
The conclusion is stronger than "$\pi_i(\Omega, \Omega^d) = 0$": homotopies relative to the whole part already in $\Omega^d$, at all base points, for every compact $P$ of small dimension.
No reparametrization $F \circ E$ is needed: Lemma 22.5 is used below a level (V13.14). Paths are functions on $\mathbb R$, so the final homotopy is corrected on paths at distance $0$.

items.title: The inclusion $\Omega^d \to \Omega$ on homotopy groups

milnor.label: §22, p. 118
milnor.statement: It follows (from the exact sequence of the pair) that the inclusion homomorphism $\pi_i\Omega^d \to \pi_i\Omega$ is an isomorphism for $i \le \lambda_0 - 2$; it is onto for $i = \lambda_0 - 1$.

lean.statement: For a slice submanifold $N$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, with the induced metric, $p, q \in N$ and $\Omega = \Omega(N; p, q)$ with Milnor's metric (V10.1), under the hypotheses of V13.2: at every $\gamma \in \Omega^d$ the inclusion induces a bijection $\pi_i(\Omega^d, \gamma) \to \pi_i(\Omega, \gamma)$ for $i \le \lambda_0 - 2$ and a surjection for $i \le \lambda_0 - 1$, $\pi_0$ included; for $i \ge 1$ the induced map is a homomorphism, hence an isomorphism.

chips: under the retract hypothesis of V13.2
diff: Inherits the hypothesis of V13.2. No exact sequence of the pair: compressing cubes gives surjectivity and compressing cylinders $I \times I^i$ injectivity.

items.title: Corollary 22.2

milnor.label: §22, Corollary 22.2
milnor.statement: With the hypotheses of Theorem 22.1, $\pi_i\Omega^d$ is isomorphic to $\pi_{i+1}M$ for $0 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 2$. Proof: $\pi_i\Omega^d \cong \pi_i\Omega$, and $\pi_i\Omega \cong \pi_{i+1}M$.

lean.statement: For a slice submanifold $N$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, with the induced metric, $p, q \in N$ and $\Omega = \Omega(N; p, q)$ with Milnor's metric (V10.1), under the hypotheses of V13.2: for every $\gamma \in \Omega^d$ there is a bijection $\pi_i(\Omega^d, \gamma) \cong \pi_{i+1}(N, p)$ for $i \le \lambda_0 - 2$, and a surjection $\pi_i(\Omega^d, \gamma) \to \pi_{i+1}(N, p)$ for $i \le \lambda_0 - 1$.

chips: under the retract hypothesis of V13.2
diff: $\pi_i(\Omega, \gamma)$ is at a minimal geodesic while $\pi_i(\Omega M) \cong \pi_{i+1}M$ concerns the constant loop: the bijection passes through Theorem 17.1 (V10.19), $\delta \mapsto \delta\cdot\gamma^{-1}$, and a change of basepoint from $\gamma\cdot\gamma^{-1}$ to the constant loop. Using $\gamma$ itself, no connectedness of $N$ is needed.
The surjection one degree higher is not in Milnor's 22.2; it follows from the surjectivity in V13.3.

items.title: Corollary 22.2 as groups; change of basepoint is a homomorphism

milnor.label: §22, Corollary 22.2
milnor.statement: The isomorphisms of Corollary 22.2 are isomorphisms of groups for $i \ge 1$.

lean.statement: For a path $\omega$ from $y_0$ to $y_1$ in any space and $i \ge 1$, change of basepoint along $\omega$ is a group isomorphism $\pi_i(Y, y_0) \cong \pi_i(Y, y_1)$. For a slice submanifold $N$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, with the induced metric, $p, q \in N$ and $\Omega = \Omega(N; p, q)$ with Milnor's metric (V10.1): $\pi_{j+1}(\Omega, \gamma) \cong \pi_{j+2}(N, p)$ as groups for every $\gamma \in \Omega$; under the hypotheses of V13.2, $\pi_i(\Omega^d, \gamma) \cong \pi_{i+1}(N, p)$ as groups for $1 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 2$, with a surjective homomorphism for $1 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 1$.

chips: under the retract hypothesis of V13.2
diff: That the change of basepoint hidden in "$\pi_i\Omega \cong \pi_{i+1}M$" is a homomorphism is proved through the free path space: $(\mathrm{ev}_1)_* = c_\omega\circ(\mathrm{ev}_0)_*$ with $(\mathrm{ev}_0)_*$ onto and both evaluations homomorphisms.

items.title: Lemma A: the minimal geodesics between antipodes are the equator

milnor.label: §22, proof of Corollary 22.3, p. 119
milnor.statement: Let $p, q = -p$ be antipodal on $S^{n+1}$. Then the space $\Omega^{\pi^2}$ of minimal geodesics from $p$ to $q$ "can be identified with" the equator $S^n$. (The exposition states this as Lemma A, with the list of all geodesics from $p$ to $-p$.)

lean.statement: On the unit sphere $S^{n+1} \subseteq \mathbb R^{n+2}$: every geodesic from $p$ to $-p$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with $t \mapsto \cos(Lt)p + \sin(Lt)u$, $u \perp p$ a unit vector, $L = (2m + 1)\pi$, and each of these is one; every path from $p$ to $-p$ has energy $\ge \pi^2$; the paths of least energy are the semicircles $\gamma_u$ ($L = \pi$), $u$ in the equator. $u \mapsto \gamma_u$ is continuous for Milnor's metric, a homotopy equivalence from the equator to $\Omega^d$ with homotopy inverse $\gamma \mapsto \gamma(\frac12)$, and a homeomorphism of the equator onto the separation quotient of $\Omega^d$.

chips: a homotopy equivalence on the nose
diff: Paths are functions on $\mathbb R$ and Milnor's metric does not see their values off $[0, 1]$, so $\Omega^d$ is homeomorphic to the equator only after identifying paths at distance $0$; the homotopy equivalence is what the homotopy groups need.
Continuity: all semicircles have speed $\pi$, so the $L^2$ part of Milnor's metric vanishes on them.

items.title: Lemma B: the index of a geodesic between antipodes

milnor.label: §22, proof of Corollary 22.3, p. 119
milnor.statement: Every non-minimal geodesic from $p$ to $-p$ must wind one and a half times around $S^{n+1}$, and therefore has index $\ge 2n$ (it passes through two conjugate points of multiplicity $n$ in its interior).

lean.statement: The geodesic $t \mapsto \cos((2m + 1)\pi t)p + \sin((2m + 1)\pi t)u$ from $p$ to $-p$ on $S^{n+1}$ has index $2mn$; every geodesic from $p$ to $-p$ not of least energy has index $\ge 2n$.

diff: By the index theorem (V9.24): the parameters $j/(2m + 1)$, $1 \le j \le 2m$, each of multiplicity $n$ (V10.23); the end point $t = 1$ is conjugate but does not count.

items.title: The neighbourhood retraction for the sphere

milnor.label: §22, proof of Corollary 22.3, p. 119
milnor.statement: "Evidently the hypotheses of Theorem 22.1 are satisfied with $\lambda_0 = 2n$": $\Omega^d \cong S^n$ is a manifold. No retraction is written down.

lean.statement: In $\Omega(S^{n+1}; p, -p)$, the set $O$ of paths with $\omega(\frac12) \neq \pm p$ is open and contains $\Omega^d$; $\omega \mapsto$ the semicircle through the normalized component of $\omega(\frac12)$ orthogonal to $p$, changed to the identity on $\Omega^d$, is a retraction of $O$ onto $\Omega^d$, continuous on $O$.

diff: This proves the hypothesis of V13.2 for the sphere, so Corollary 22.3 does not depend on Hanner's theorem.

items.title: Corollary 22.3 (Freudenthal)

milnor.label: §22, Corollary 22.3
milnor.statement: $\pi_iS^n \cong \pi_{i+1}S^{n+1}$ for $i \le 2n - 2$.

lean.statement: For all $x \in S^n$, $y \in S^{n+1}$: $\pi_i(S^n, x) \cong \pi_{i+1}(S^{n+1}, y)$ for $i \le 2n - 2$ (a bijection), as groups for $1 \le i \le 2n - 2$; and for $i \le 2n - 1$ a surjection $\pi_i(S^n, x) \to \pi_{i+1}(S^{n+1}, y)$, a homomorphism for $i \ge 1$.

diff: The second half of Freudenthal's theorem, the surjection for $i = 2n - 1$, is not in Milnor's 22.3; it follows from the surjectivity in V13.3 (his remark on $\pi_{\lambda_0 - 1}$).
Unconditional: the retraction is V13.8, and the equator is $S^n$ by an isometry of $p^\perp$ with $\mathbb R^{n+1}$. That the isomorphism is the suspension homomorphism is not formalized.

items.title: Lemma 22.4

milnor.label: §22, Lemma 22.4
milnor.statement: Let $K$ be a compact subset of an open $U \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ and $f : U \to \mathbb R$ smooth, all of whose critical points in $K$ have index $\ge \lambda_0$. If $g : U \to \mathbb R$ is smooth and its first and second partial derivatives are within $\varepsilon$ of those of $f$ uniformly on $K$, $\varepsilon$ small, then every critical point of $g$ in $K$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$. Proof (pp. 120–121): the $\lambda$-th eigenvalue of the Hessian is continuous, and "a uniform continuity argument which will be left to the reader".

lean.statement: Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed space, $K \subseteq U \subseteq E$ with $K$ compact and $U$ open, and $f : E \to \mathbb R$ of class $C^2$ on $U$ with every critical point in $K$ of index $\ge \lambda_0$. There is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every $g$ with $\|dg_x - df_x\| < \varepsilon$ and $\|d^2g_x - d^2f_x\| < \varepsilon$ (operator norms) at each $x \in K$ has all its critical points in $K$ of index $\ge \lambda_0$; likewise for $g = f + h$ with the first two derivatives of $h$ smaller than $\varepsilon$ on $K$.

diff: Closeness is measured by operator norms of $dg - df$ and $d^2g - d^2f$, equivalent to Milnor's partial derivatives up to constants; $f$ need only be $C^2$ and may have degenerate critical points, as Theorem 22.1 needs.

The proof uses no eigenvalues: a negative definite subspace keeps a margin $\mu$ and stays negative definite under perturbations smaller than $\mu$; compactness of $K$ is the "uniform continuity argument".

items.title: Lemma 22.4 on a submanifold, for linear perturbations

milnor.label: §22, proof of Lemma 22.5, p. 122
milnor.statement: In the proof of Lemma 22.5: $g$ is chosen with first and second derivatives so close to those of $f$ that Lemma 22.4 applies "in a coordinate neighbourhood" of each point of a compact set.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq V$ be a slice submanifold, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth and $K \subseteq N$ compact, with every critical point of $F|N$ in $K$ of index $\ge \lambda_0$. There is $\delta > 0$ such that for every linear form $a$ on $V$ with $\|a\| < \delta$, every critical point of $(F + a)|N$ in $K$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$.

diff: Only linear perturbations: those by which Corollary 6.8 (V4.22) produces Morse functions, which is what Lemma 22.5 needs. Finitely many slice charts cover $K$.

items.title: Pushing maps, and pushing off cells

milnor.label: §22, proof of Lemma 22.5, p. 122
milnor.statement: "Since $r < \lambda_0$ it follows that $h$ is homotopic within $(M^c, M^0)$ to a map $h'$ into $g^{-1}(-\infty, 2\delta]$": maps of dimension below $\lambda_0$ can be pushed off cells of dimension $\ge \lambda_0$.

lean.statement: $A$ pushes maps from $P$ out of $X$ ($A, X \subseteq T$) if every map $P \to T$ with values in $X$ is homotopic in $T$, relative to the preimage of $A$, to a map into $A$. This is transitive and monotone; a strong deformation retract pushes maps from every $P$; and if $T$ is Hausdorff, $A$ closed, $P$ compact with a continuous injection into a real vector space of dimension $d$, and $e_1, \dots, e_k$ are disjoint embedded closed cells of dimensions $> d$ meeting $A$ exactly in their boundary spheres, then $A$ pushes maps from $P$ out of $A \cup e_1 \cup \dots \cup e_k$.

diff: The notion replaces relative homotopy groups throughout §22. One cell is the compression lemma for attaching a cell (Hatcher, Lemma 4.10), which Milnor uses without comment.

items.title: Lemma D: passing critical levels of high index

milnor.label: §22, proof of Lemma 22.5, p. 122
milnor.statement: $g$ has only non-degenerate critical points, of index $\ge \lambda_0$, in $g^{-1}[2\delta, c + \delta]$; so $g^{-1}(-\infty, c + \delta]$ has the homotopy type of $g^{-1}(-\infty, 2\delta]$ with cells of dimension $\ge \lambda_0$ attached.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq V$ be a slice submanifold, $F : V \to \mathbb R$ smooth, $f = F|N$, $f^{-1}(-\infty, a_0]$ compact, $a$ a regular value, and every critical point $q$ with $a < f(q) \le a_0$ non-degenerate of index $\ge \lambda_0$. For $P$ compact injected into a real vector space of dimension $< \lambda_0$ and $a \le b < a_0$, $N^a$ pushes maps from $P$ out of $N^b$.

diff: A homotopy type alone would not do: the argument needs the deformations of Theorem 3.1 and Remark 3.3 (V2.3, V2.9), which fix the lower level, and V13.12 for the cells.
The critical points above $a$ are finitely many: isolated in a compact set, and not accumulating at the regular level $a$. Milnor does not say so.

items.title: Lemma 22.5

milnor.label: §22, Lemma 22.5
milnor.statement: Let $f : M \to \mathbb R$ be smooth with minimum $0$ and each $M^c = f^{-1}[0, c]$ compact. If the set $M^0$ of minimal points is a manifold and every critical point in $M - M^0$ has index $\ge \lambda_0$, then $\pi_r(M, M^0) = 0$ for $0 \le r < \lambda_0$. Proof (pp. 121–122): by Hanner, $M^0$ is a retract of a neighbourhood $U$ which deforms into $M^0$; a smooth approximation $g$ of $f$ pushes $h$ into $U$.

lean.statement: Let $N \subseteq V$ be a slice submanifold, $F$ smooth, $f = F|N \ge d$, $M^0 = f^{-1}(d)$, $P$ compact injected into a real vector space of dimension $< \lambda_0$, and $U \supseteq M^0$ open with $M^0$ pushing maps from $P$ out of $U$ (e.g. $U$ deforms into $M^0$ fixing it). (i) If $f^{-1}(-\infty, a_0]$ is compact and the critical points with $d < f < a_0$ have index $\ge \lambda_0$, $M^0$ pushes maps from $P$ out of $f^{-1}(-\infty, b]$ for every $b < a_0$. (ii) With all sublevel sets compact and every critical point off $M^0$ of index $\ge \lambda_0$, $M^0$ pushes maps from $P$ out of $N$.

diff: The conclusion of Milnor's first step (Hanner's theorem plus short geodesics) is a hypothesis.

Milnor's $g$ lives on the compact $M^{c + 2\delta}$, too little for Theorems 3.1 and 3.2; here $g = F + \rho\ell$ with $\ell$ a small linear form making $(F + \ell)|N$ Morse and $\rho$ a bump function, and the lower level is chosen regular ($2\delta$ might be critical). $M^0$ compact is implicit in the book.

items.title: Deforming a neighbourhood of the minimal geodesics

milnor.label: §22, proof of Lemma 22.5, p. 121
milnor.statement: "$M^0$ is a retract of some neighborhood $U$ … taking $U$ small, we may assume that each point of $U$ is joined to its image under the retraction by a unique minimal geodesic; hence $U$ can be deformed into $M^0$ within $M$."

lean.statement: In the finite-dimensional model of Chapter 10 (a broken-geodesic setup with energy bound $c$), let $N^m \cap O$, $O$ open, consist of admissible break points, and $d < c$. If $\{\gamma : E(\gamma) \le d\}$ is a retract of an open set of $\Omega$ containing it, then $\{y \in N^m \cap O : E'(y) \le d\}$ has an open neighbourhood in $N^m \cap O$ from which it pushes maps from every $P$.

chips: the retraction transported to break points
diff: Each break point moves to that of the retracted path along the short geodesic of Corollary 10.8; the deformation stays in the open manifold $N^m \cap O$ near $M^0$ by the tube lemma; the retraction in $\Omega$ is transported to break points.

items.title: Theorem 22.1 for an open and closed set of paths

milnor.label: §24, p. 147
milnor.statement: In the case $k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$ of §24: "we will need a variant of Theorem 22.1 for the component $\Omega^{(c)}$ of the path space". (The exposition states it as Lemma 6.2 of its Chapter 15.)

lean.statement: For a slice submanifold $N$ of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$, with the induced metric, $p, q \in N$ and $\Omega = \Omega(N; p, q)$ with Milnor's metric (V10.1), under the compact-ball and retract hypotheses of V13.2, let $\Omega' \subseteq \Omega$ be open and closed with every geodesic in $\Omega'$ not of least energy of index $\ge \lambda_0$. Then every map $h : P \to \Omega'$ is homotopic, relative to $h^{-1}(\Omega^d)$, to a map into $\Omega^d \cap \Omega'$; the inclusion $\Omega^d \cap \Omega' \to \Omega'$ is bijective on $\pi_i$, $i \le \lambda_0 - 2$, and $\Omega^d \to \Omega$ is bijective on $\pi_i$, $1 \le i \le \lambda_0 - 2$, at the points of $\Omega^d \cap \Omega'$.

chips: under the retract hypothesis of V13.2
diff: Where the proof of 22.1 must see $\Omega'$ is made explicit: $r_u$ keeps a path in its component, the manifold of break points is cut down to the paths in $\Omega'$, and the last homotopy stays there. $d$ is the least energy on all of $\Omega$, and $\Omega'$ need not contain a minimal geodesic.

milnor.label: §23, p. 127
milnor.statement: For $A = \operatorname{diag}(ia_1, \dots, ia_n)$, $\exp A = \operatorname{diag}(e^{ia_1}, \dots, e^{ia_n})$, so $\exp A = -I$ iff $A = \operatorname{diag}(k_1i\pi, \dots, k_ni\pi)$ with odd integers $k_j$; a general skew-Hermitian $A$ is first conjugated to diagonal form (pp. 126–127).

lean.statement: For real $a$, $e^{ia} = -1$ iff $a$ is $\pi$ times an odd integer; so $\exp\operatorname{diag}(ia_1, \dots, ia_n) = -I$ iff every $a_j$ is an odd multiple of $\pi$.

items.title: Length and trace of the velocity

milnor.label: §23, pp. 127, 130
milnor.statement: The geodesic $t \mapsto \exp tA$ has length $|A| = \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}AA^*} = \pi\sqrt{k_1^2 + \dots + k_n^2}$; $A$ lies in the Lie algebra of $SU(n)$ iff the odd $k_j$ have sum zero.

lean.statement: For integers $k_j$ and $A = \operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_j)$: $\operatorname{tr}(AA^*) = \pi^2\sum k_j^2$ and $\operatorname{tr}A = i\pi\sum k_j$.

milnor.label: §23, p. 127
milnor.statement: $A$ determines a minimal geodesic iff each $k_j = \pm1$; in $SU(2m)$ the condition $\operatorname{tr}A = 0$ makes $\operatorname{Eigen}(i\pi)$ $m$-dimensional.

lean.statement: For odd $k_1, \dots, k_n$, $\sum k_j^2 \ge n$, with equality iff every $k_j = \pm1$; if $n = 2m$, all $k_j = \pm1$ and $\sum k_j = 0$, then $m$ of them are $1$ and $m$ are $-1$.

items.title: Lemma 23.1 as a statement about projections

milnor.label: §23, pp. 127–128
milnor.statement: A minimal $A$ is completely determined by $\operatorname{Eigen}(i\pi)$, an arbitrary subspace, of dimension $m$ in $SU(2m)$.

lean.statement: A skew-Hermitian $A$ has $A^2 = -\pi^2I$ iff $A = i\pi(2P - I)$ for a Hermitian projection $P$; $\operatorname{tr}(i\pi(2P - I)) = i\pi(2\operatorname{tr}P - n)$.

diff: "Completely determined by $\operatorname{Eigen}(i\pi)$" uses that $A$ is normal; the identity gives the projection without the spectral theorem.

items.title: The operator $K_A$ for diagonal $A$

milnor.label: §23, pp. 130–131
milnor.statement: By Theorem 20.5 the conjugate points are determined by $K_A(W) = R(A, W)A = \frac14[[A, W], A]$; a short computation gives $K_A(W) = (\frac{\pi^2}4(k_j - k_l)^2w_{jl})$.

lean.statement: With $K_A(W) = \frac14[[A, W], A]$: for $A = \operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_j)$ the $(j, l)$ entry of $K_A(W)$ is $\frac{\pi^2}4(k_j - k_l)^2w_{jl}$.

diff: That it is $W \mapsto R(A, W)A$ for $SU(n)$ is V12.17.

items.title: Milnor's eigenvectors, and that they span

milnor.label: §23, p. 131
milnor.statement: A basis of the Lie algebra of $SU(n)$ of eigenvectors of $K_A$: $E_{jl}$ and $E'_{jl}$, $j < l$, with eigenvalue $\frac{\pi^2}4(k_j - k_l)^2$, and the diagonal matrices, with eigenvalue $0$.

lean.statement: $E_{jl}$ ($1$ at $(j, l)$, $-1$ at $(l, j)$) and $E'_{jl}$ ($i$ at both) are skew-Hermitian, traceless for $j \neq l$, and eigenvectors of $K_A$ with eigenvalue $\frac{\pi^2}4(k_j - k_l)^2$; diagonal matrices are in the kernel; every skew-Hermitian $W$ is its diagonal part plus $\sum_{j<l}(\operatorname{Re}w_{jl}E_{jl} + \operatorname{Im}w_{jl}E'_{jl})$.

diff: Milnor does not say why these vectors span; linear independence is not formalized. The formal index computation (V14.18–V14.19) needs no eigenbasis.

items.title: Conjugate parameters of an eigenvalue: Theorem 20.5 as a definition

milnor.label: §20, Theorem 20.5, p. 110; §23, p. 131
milnor.statement: Each eigenvalue $e > 0$ gives conjugate points at $t = \pi/\sqrt e, 2\pi/\sqrt e, \dots$; here $t = 2/(k_j - k_l), 4/(k_j - k_l), \dots$, and the number in $(0, 1)$ is "evidently" $(k_j - k_l)/2 - 1$.

lean.statement: The conjugate parameters of $e$ are the $t \in (0, 1)$ of the form $\pi s/\sqrt e$, $s \in \mathbb Z$ (none if $e \le 0$); a finite set, equal to $\{1/d, \dots, (d - 1)/d\}$ for $e = (\pi d)^2$, $d \ge 1$.

diff: Theorem 20.5 is its conclusion taken as a definition; for $SU(n)$ the theorem is V14.18. "Evidently" needs $k_j - k_l$ even.

items.title: The index of a spectrum: Theorems 20.5 and 15.1 as a definition

milnor.label: §23, p. 131
milnor.statement: Applying the Index Theorem and "adding over all $j, l$".

lean.statement: For a finite family $e = (e_i)$ of reals, the multiplicity of $t$ is the number of $i$ with $t$ a conjugate parameter of $e_i$, and the index of $e$ is the sum of the multiplicities; it equals $\sum_i\#\{\text{conjugate parameters of } e_i\}$; doubling every value doubles it.

diff: "Adding over all $j, l$" exchanges two finite sums.

items.title: The index formula from Milnor's spectrum

milnor.label: §23, p. 131
milnor.statement: $\lambda = \sum_{k_j > k_l}(k_j - k_l - 2)$: each pair $k_j > k_l$ gives two copies of $\frac{\pi^2}4(k_j - k_l)^2$, contributing $2((k_j - k_l)/2 - 1)$.

lean.statement: Put $\operatorname{bott}(k) = \sum_{k_i > k_j}(k_i - k_j - 2)$. For odd $k_j$, the index (V14.8) of the spectrum consisting of $\frac{\pi^2}4(k_i - k_j)^2$ for each pair $k_i > k_j$, each twice, is $\operatorname{bott}(k)$.

items.title: Elementary properties of the index formula

milnor.label: §23, pp. 130–132
milnor.statement: Milnor normalizes $k_1 \ge \dots \ge k_n$, treats "(say) negative" by symmetry, and notes that a minimal geodesic (all $k_j = \pm1$) has index $0$.

lean.statement: For odd $k_j$, $\operatorname{bott}(k) \ge 0$; $\operatorname{bott}(-k) = \operatorname{bott}(k)$; $\operatorname{bott}$ does not depend on the order; and it is $0$ if every $k_j = \pm1$.

items.title: Lemma 23.2, combinatorially

milnor.label: §23, Lemma 23.2, p. 128; proof p. 132
milnor.statement: Every non-minimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(2m)$ has index $\ge 2m + 2$. Proof (p. 132): Case 1, at least $m + 1$ of the $k_j$ (say) negative; Case 2, $m$ of each sign, not all $\pm1$.

lean.statement: For odd $k_1, \dots, k_{2m}$ with $\sum k_j = 0$, not all $\pm1$: $\operatorname{bott}(k) \ge 2m + 2$.

diff: Both cases through the sum over pairs (positive $k_i$, negative $k_j$), reproducing Milnor's bounds $2N$ and $4m$; his "one is $\ge 3$" uses $\sum k_j = 0$.

items.title: Why $SU(2m)$ and not $U(n)$

milnor.label: §23, p. 127
milnor.statement: The space of minimal geodesics in $U(n)$ is "rather inconvenient", having components of varying dimensions; so Milnor passes to $SU(2m)$.

lean.statement: For $k = (3, 1, \dots, 1) \in \mathbb Z^{n+1}$: $\operatorname{bott}(k) = 0$, not every $k_j = \pm1$, and $\sum k_j = n + 3$, whereas every family of entries $\pm1$ has $|\sum k_j|$ at most the number of entries.

diff: The exposition's stronger reason: this non-minimal geodesic has index $0$ in a component of the path space without minimal geodesics. That $\sum k_j$ is constant on components is not formalized.

items.title: $U(n)$ and $SU(n)$ as compact matrix groups

milnor.label: §23, pp. 124–126
milnor.statement: $U(n)$ is a compact smooth submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb C)$ and a Lie group, with tangent space $\mathfrak u(n)$ (skew-Hermitian matrices) at $I$ (Milnor's (5), (6), using $\exp$ near $0$ as a chart); its Lie bracket is the commutator and $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{tr}(AB^*)$ gives a bi-invariant metric; $\det\exp A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$, and $SU(n)$ has Lie algebra $\mathfrak{su}(n)$.

lean.statement: $U(n)$ is a compact slice submanifold of $M_n(\mathbb C)$ modelled on $\mathfrak u(n)$, a regular level set of $A \mapsto A^*A - I$, and a matrix group (V12.14) with $\mathfrak u(n)$; for $n \ge 1$, $SU(n)$ is a compact slice submanifold modelled on $\mathfrak{su}(n)$ and a matrix group with $\mathfrak{su}(n)$. Jacobi's formula $d(\det)_A(AX) = \det A\operatorname{tr}X$, and $\det\exp(tX) = 1$ for $\operatorname{tr}X = 0$.

diff: $SU(n)$ is not a regular level set of $(A^*A - I, \det A - 1)$; it is the open piece $\operatorname{Re}\det > 0$ of the regular level set $\{A^*A = I, \operatorname{Im}\det A = 0\}$.
Only the traceless case of $\det\exp A = e^{\operatorname{tr}A}$ is proved. That $\exp$ is onto and $SU(n)$ connected is not formalized (not needed).

milnor.label: §23, pp. 126–127, 130
milnor.statement: A geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ is $t \mapsto \exp tA$ with $\exp A = -I$; after conjugation by a unitary $T$, $A = \operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_j)$ with odd $k_j$, and in $SU(n)$ with $\sum k_j = 0$.

lean.statement: Every geodesic of $SU(n)$ on $[0, 1]$ starting at $I$ agrees there with $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$, $A \in \mathfrak{su}(n)$. If $A \in \mathfrak{su}(n)$ and $\exp A = -I$, then $A = T\operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_j)T^*$ with $T$ unitary, $k_j$ odd and $\sum k_j = 0$; conversely such $A$ lies in $\mathfrak{su}(n)$, $\exp A = -I$, and $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ is a geodesic from $I$ to $-I$.

items.title: The distance from $I$ to $-I$, and the minimal geodesics

milnor.label: §23, p. 127
milnor.statement: The geodesic $t \mapsto \exp tA$ has length $\pi(\sum k_j^2)^{1/2}$; it is minimal iff every $k_j = \pm1$.

lean.statement: For skew-Hermitian $A$ the length of $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ on $[0, 1]$ is $\|A\|$, which is $\pi(\sum k_j^2)^{1/2} \ge \pi\sqrt n$ for $A = T\operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_j)T^*$, $k_j$ odd. In $SU(2m)$, $m \ge 1$: $\rho(I, -I) = \pi\sqrt{2m}$, and for $A \in \mathfrak{su}(2m)$ with $\exp A = -I$ the geodesic $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ is minimal iff $A^2 = -\pi^2I$, iff all $k_j = \pm1$.

diff: That a geodesic of length $\pi\sqrt n$ is minimal needs a shortest geodesic to exist (Hopf–Rinow, in the compact group) and every geodesic from $I$ to be an $\exp(tA)$ (V12.15). Only $SU(2m)$, the case used, is treated.

items.title: Lemma 23.1: the velocities of the minimal geodesics form $G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$

milnor.label: §23, Lemma 23.1
milnor.statement: The space of minimal geodesics from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(2m)$ is homeomorphic to the complex Grassmann manifold $G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$.

lean.statement: Let $|\iota| = 2m$ and $\operatorname{minVel} = \{A \in \mathfrak{su}(2m) : A^2 = -\pi^2I\}$. Then $A \in \operatorname{minVel}$ iff $\exp A = -I$ and $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ is a minimal geodesic; and $A \mapsto \frac12(I - \frac i\pi A)$ is a homeomorphism of $\operatorname{minVel}$ onto $G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$, the Hermitian projections of trace $m$, with inverse $P \mapsto i\pi(2P - I)$.

diff: Milnor matches the two spaces only as sets (`Exposition/Findings.md`); here the topology is that of matrices. The space of paths is V14.17.

items.title: Lemma 23.1 in the path space

milnor.label: §23, Lemma 23.1
milnor.statement: The space of minimal geodesics from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(2m)$ (as a subspace of $\Omega$) is homeomorphic to $G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$.

lean.statement: Let $|\iota| = 2m$. Every path from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(2m)$ has energy $\ge 2m\pi^2$; for $A \in \operatorname{minVel}$, $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ lies in $\Omega^d$, and every $\gamma \in \Omega^d$ agrees on $[0, 1]$ with one of these, $A = \pi\gamma(\frac12)$. $A \mapsto (t \mapsto \exp tA)$ is continuous for Milnor's metric and is a homotopy equivalence $\operatorname{minVel} \simeq \Omega^d$ (inverse $\gamma \mapsto \pi\gamma(\frac12)$), and a homeomorphism onto the separation quotient of $\Omega^d$.

chips: a homotopy equivalence on the nose
diff: Paths are functions on $\mathbb R$, so $\Omega^d$ is homeomorphic to $G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$ only after identifying paths agreeing on $[0, 1]$; the homotopy equivalence is what Theorem 23.3 uses.
Continuity for Milnor's metric: all minimal geodesics have speed $\pi\sqrt{2m}$, so the $L^2$ part vanishes, and $\exp(A/2) = A/\pi$ recovers the velocity from the midpoint.

items.title: Theorem 20.5 for $SU(n)$

milnor.label: §20, Theorem 20.5, p. 110; §23, pp. 130–131
milnor.statement: By Theorem 20.5 the conjugate points along $t \mapsto \exp tA$ are determined by the eigenvalues of $K_A(W) = \frac14[[A, W], A]$: an eigenvalue $e > 0$ gives conjugate points at the multiples of $\pi/\sqrt e$, the multiplicity counting the eigenvalues; "adding over all $j, l$".

lean.statement: For $A = T\operatorname{diag}(ia_j)T^* \in \mathfrak{su}(n)$, $T$ unitary, and $C \in \mathfrak{su}(n)$, $J_C(t) = e^{tA/2}T(S(t) \odot T^*CT)T^*e^{tA/2}$, with $S(t) \odot W$ the matrix of $\frac{\sin(b_{jl}t)}{b_{jl}}w_{jl}$, $b_{jl} = (a_j - a_l)/2$, is a Jacobi field along $\exp(tA)$ with $J_C(0) = 0$, $DJ_C/dt(0) = C$. The multiplicity of $t_0 \in [0, 1]$ as a parameter conjugate to $0$ is $\dim\{W \in \mathfrak{su}(n) : S(t_0) \odot W = 0\}$, which for $a = \pi k$ and $0 < t_0 < 1$ equals the multiplicity computed from Milnor's spectrum (V14.8–V14.9).

diff: The multiplicity is the dimension of a space of Jacobi fields, so all Jacobi fields vanishing at $0$ must be described: here explicitly, entry by entry, in the frame of V12.18, and by uniqueness.
Milnor's reduction to diagonal $A$ by an isometry fixing $\pm I$ (p. 130) is replaced by carrying $T$ through the computation.

items.title: The index of a geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(n)$

milnor.label: §23, p. 131
milnor.statement: By the Index Theorem, the index of $t \mapsto \exp tA$, $0 \le t \le 1$, is $\lambda = \sum_{k_j > k_l}(k_j - k_l - 2)$.

lean.statement: For integers $k_j$ with $\sum k_j = 0$, $T$ unitary and $A = T\operatorname{diag}(i\pi k_j)T^*$ with $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ a path from $I$ to $-I$, the index of $E_{**}$ at this geodesic is the index of Milnor's spectrum; hence every geodesic $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(n)$ has index $\sum_{k_i > k_j}(k_i - k_j - 2)$ for its odd $k_j$ (V14.14).

items.title: Lemma 23.2 for geodesics

milnor.label: §23, Lemma 23.2
milnor.statement: Every non-minimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(2m)$ has index $\ge 2m + 2$.

lean.statement: Let $|\iota| = 2m$. A geodesic $t \mapsto \exp(tA)$ from $I$ to $-I$ in $SU(2m)$ has index $0$ if all $k_j = \pm1$ and $\ge 2m + 2$ otherwise; every geodesic of $\Omega(SU(2m); I, -I)$ not of least energy has index $\ge 2m + 2$.

diff: The last clause is the index hypothesis of Theorem 22.1 (V13.2) with $\lambda_0 = 2m + 2$.

items.title: The neighbourhood retraction for $SU(2m)$, and Corollary 22.2 for it

milnor.label: §23, p. 128
milnor.statement: By Lemma 23.1, $\Omega^d$ is a manifold, and by Lemma 23.2 every non-minimal geodesic has index $\ge 2m + 2$; with Theorem 22.1 this gives the result. No retraction is written down.

lean.statement: Let $|\iota| = 2m$. With $Q(H)$ the spectral projection of a Hermitian $H$ onto the eigenvalues $> \frac12$ (continuous where $\frac12$ is not an eigenvalue), the paths $\omega$ for which $\frac12$ is not an eigenvalue of $H(\omega)$, the Hermitian part of $\frac12(I - i\omega(\frac12))$, and $|\operatorname{tr}Q(H(\omega)) - m| < \frac12$ form an open set $O \supseteq \Omega^d$, and $\omega \mapsto (t \mapsto \exp(t\,i\pi(2Q - I)))$, changed to the identity on $\Omega^d$, retracts $O$ onto $\Omega^d$. Hence $\pi_i(\Omega^d, \gamma) \cong \pi_{i+1}(SU(2m), I)$ for $i \le 2m$, as groups for $1 \le i \le 2m$.

chips: Hanner replaced by a spectral projection
diff: This proves the hypothesis of V13.2 for $SU(2m)$, so Theorem 23.3 is unconditional. The trace is locally constant on projections, which keeps the rank $m$.

items.title: Theorem 23.3 (Bott)

milnor.label: §23, Theorem 23.3
milnor.statement: The inclusion $G_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \to \Omega(SU(2m); I, -I)$ induces isomorphisms of homotopy groups in dimensions $\le 2m$. Hence $\pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i+1}SU(2m)$ for $0 \le i \le 2m$.

lean.statement: Let $|\iota| = 2m$. For every $P \in G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$ and $i \le 2m$ there is a bijection $\pi_i(G_m(\mathbb C^{2m}), P) \cong \pi_{i+1}(SU(2m), I)$, and a group isomorphism for $1 \le i \le 2m$.

diff: The isomorphism is the composite of Lemma 23.1 (V14.16), the homotopy equivalence of V14.17 and Corollary 22.2 for $SU(2m)$ (V14.21). The statement about the inclusion is V13.3 for $\Omega^d$ with $\lambda_0 = 2m + 2$, $\Omega^d$ being identified with $G_m$ by V14.16–V14.17.
Theorem 22.1 is proved as a compression, which gives bijections; group isomorphisms in the degrees where both sides are groups need change of basepoint to be a homomorphism (V13.5).

items.title: Coset bundles: local sections, Stiefel manifolds, $U(m + 1) \to S^{2m+1}$

milnor.label: §23, pp. 128–129
milnor.statement: $U(m + 1)/U(m) \cong S^{2m+1}$; the complex Stiefel manifold $U(2m)/U(m)$; the fibrations $U(m) \to U(m + 1) \to S^{2m+1}$ and $U(m) \to U(2m) \to U(2m)/U(m)$, from Steenrod (a coset map with local cross-sections is a bundle).

lean.statement: An equivariant map onto a space with a transitive group action is locally trivial with fibre the fibre over $b_0$ if the orbit map at $b_0$ has a continuous local section. $U(n)$ acts transitively on the Stiefel manifold $V_k(\mathbb K^n) = \{F : F^*F = I\}$, with an explicit continuous local section near the base frame. Restricting frames to their last vectors is locally trivial with fibre a Stiefel manifold, $g \mapsto gF_0$, $U(n) \to V_k(\mathbb K^n)$, is locally trivial with fibre $U(n - k)$, and $V_1(\mathbb K^n)$ is the unit sphere, so $U(m + 1) \to S^{2m+1}$ is locally trivial with fibre $U(m)$.

diff: No coset space appears: the bundles are orbit maps between spaces of matrices, with the local section written down. Locally trivial maps are Serre fibrations with an exact homotopy sequence (Part XII).

milnor.label: §23, p. 129
milnor.statement: $G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$ can be identified with $U(2m)/U(m) \times U(m)$, and there is a fibration $U(m) \to U(2m)/U(m) \to G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$.

lean.statement: Every $P \in G_m(\mathbb K^n)$ (Hermitian projections of trace $m$) is $FF^*$ for an orthonormal $m$-frame; $F \mapsto FF^*$, $V_m(\mathbb K^n) \to G_m(\mathbb K^n)$, is continuous, equivariant for the transitive action $P \mapsto gPg^*$, and locally trivial with fibre $U(m)$, the local section being Gram–Schmidt. The Grassmannian of Lemma 23.1 is this one.

items.title: Lemma 23.4: stability, and the connectivity of Stiefel manifolds

milnor.label: §23, Lemma 23.4, pp. 128–129
milnor.statement: $\pi_{i-1}U(m) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m + 1) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m + 2) \cong \cdots$ for $i \le 2m$, induced by the inclusions; $\pi_{2m}U(m) \to \pi_{2m}U(m + 1)$ is onto; and $\pi_i(U(2m)/U(m)) = 0$ for $i \le 2m$.

lean.statement: $\pi_iS^{2n-1} = 0$ for $i < 2n - 1$. $\pi_iV_k(\mathbb C^n) = 0$ for $k \le n$, $i \le 2(n - k)$. The inclusion $U(m) \to U(m + k)$, $S \mapsto \operatorname{diag}(S, I_k)$, induces bijections on $\pi_i$ for $i < 2m$ and surjections for $i \le 2m$, at every base point.

diff: The connectivity of every Stiefel manifold, by induction on $k$ through the restriction bundles, instead of Milnor's exact-sequence argument for $U(2m)/U(m)$ alone.

items.title: Lemma 23.4: $\pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m)$

milnor.label: §23, Lemma 23.4
milnor.statement: For $1 \le i \le 2m$, $\pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i-1}U(m)$ (from the exact sequence of $U(m) \to U(2m)/U(m) \to G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$).

lean.statement: For $1 \le i \le 2m$ and every $P \in G_m(\mathbb C^{2m})$ there is a bijection $\pi_i(G_m(\mathbb C^{2m}), P) \cong \pi_{i-1}(U(m), I)$, a group isomorphism for $2 \le i \le 2m$; the same for the space $\operatorname{minVel}$ of V14.16.

diff: For $i = 1$ both sides are trivial, which is not stated separately; the isomorphism is the boundary map of the bundle, whose total space is $2m$-connected (V14.25), moved to any $P$ by a unitary motion.

items.title: Lemma 23.4: $\pi_jSU(m) \cong \pi_jU(m)$

milnor.label: §23, Lemma 23.4
milnor.statement: $\pi_jU(m) \cong \pi_jSU(m)$ for $j \neq 1$, from $SU(m) \to U(m) \to S^1$.

lean.statement: $U(n) \cong S^1 \times SU(n)$ by $g \mapsto (\det g, gD(\det g)^{-1})$; $\pi_jS^1 = 0$ for $j \ge 2$; and for $n \ge 1$ the inclusion $SU(n) \to U(n)$ induces bijections on $\pi_j$, $j \ge 2$, at every point.

diff: $j = 0$ (both groups connected) is not formalized and is not used.

items.title: The periodicity theorem

milnor.label: §23, p. 129
milnor.statement: Periodicity theorem: $\pi_{i-1}U \cong \pi_{i+1}U$, the stable groups $\pi_jU = \pi_jU(m)$, $j \le 2m - 1$; proof: $\pi_{i-1}U(m) \cong \pi_iG_m(\mathbb C^{2m}) \cong \pi_{i+1}SU(2m) \cong \pi_{i+1}U(2m)$ for $i \le 2m$ (Lemma 23.4, Theorem 23.3, Lemma 23.4).

lean.statement: For $1 \le i \le 2m$, $\pi_{i-1}(U(m), I) \cong \pi_{i+1}(U(2m), I)$, as groups for $2 \le i \le 2m$. For $1 \le i \le 2m - 2$, $\pi_{i-1}(U(m), I) \cong \pi_{i+1}(U(m), I)$, as groups for $2 \le i \le 2m - 2$.

diff: The stable group $\pi_jU$ is not defined as a limit; periodicity is stated inside one $U(m)$. Landing back in $U(m)$ from $U(2m)$ needs stability in degree $i + 1 < 2m$, hence $i \le 2m - 2$; every stable degree is reached for $m$ large.
For $i = 1$, $\pi_0$ is a pointed set and the isomorphism a bijection.

items.title: Theorem 23.5 (Bott), as sets

milnor.label: §23, Theorem 23.5, p. 130
milnor.statement: The stable homotopy groups of the unitary group are $\pi_0U \cong \pi_2U \cong \pi_4U \cong \cdots \cong 0$ and $\pi_1U \cong \pi_3U \cong \pi_5U \cong \cdots \cong \mathbb Z$. Proof: $U(1) = S^1$ and periodicity.

lean.statement: For $j \le 2m - 1$: $\pi_j(U(m), I)$ is trivial for even $j$ and in bijection with $\mathbb Z$ for odd $j$. On the way: $\pi_1(S^1) \cong \mathbb Z$ as sets, by the boundary map of the covering $\mathbb Z \to \mathbb R \to S^1$; $\det : U(1) \to S^1$ is a homeomorphism.

diff: Statements about $\pi_jU(m)$ for $j \le 2m - 1$ rather than a limit group; the odd groups as groups are V14.30.

items.title: Theorem 23.5 as groups

milnor.label: §23, Theorem 23.5, p. 130
milnor.statement: $\pi_1U \cong \pi_3U \cong \pi_5U \cong \cdots$ are infinite cyclic; $\pi_1S^1 \cong \mathbb Z$ is quoted.

lean.statement: $\pi_1(S^1, 1) \cong \mathbb Z$ as groups. For $2k + 2 \le 2m$, $\pi_{2k+1}(U(m), I) \cong \mathbb Z$ as groups; in the stable range $\pi_jU(m) \cong \pi_1U(m)$ for odd $j$ and $\cong \pi_2U(m)$ for even $j \ge 2$, as groups.

diff: $\pi_1S^1 \cong \mathbb Z$ comes from Mathlib's covering-space theory: the monodromy of $t \mapsto e^{it}$, whose deck group $2\pi\mathbb Z$ is abelian.

items.title: Complex structures

milnor.label: §24, p. 133
milnor.statement: For $n$ even, a complex structure on $\mathbb R^n$ is a $J \in O(n)$ with $J^2 = -I$; the space of all of them is $\Omega_1(n)$. Since $JJ^* = I$ and $JJ = -I$, $J^* = -J$ (p. 135).

lean.statement: A complex structure on $\mathbb R^n$ is a matrix $J \in O(n)$ with $J^2 = -I$. Equivalently, $J^{\mathsf T} = -J$ and $J^2 = -I$. A complex structure exists only if $n$ is even, and every complex structure has $\operatorname{tr}(J^{\mathsf T}J) = n$.

diff: Equivalently $J^{\mathsf T} = -J$ and $J^2 = -I$. The parity of $n$ is a conclusion.

items.title: $\exp(\theta J) = \cos\theta\,I + \sin\theta\,J$

milnor.label: §24, proof of Lemma 24.1, pp. 134–135
milnor.statement: In a suitable basis $\exp(\pi A)$ is block diagonal with rotation blocks; for a complex structure $J$, $\exp\pi J = -I$.

lean.statement: If $J^2 = -I$, then $\exp(\theta J) = \cos\theta\,I + \sin\theta\,J$ for every real $\theta$; in particular $\exp(\pi J) = -I$.

diff: Only the identity, for every real $\theta$. That $t \mapsto \exp(\pi tJ)$ is a minimal geodesic, and Lemma 24.1 itself, are V15.24–V15.26.

items.title: Lemma 24.2, from Milnor's spectrum

milnor.label: §24, Lemma 24.2
milnor.statement: Any non-minimal geodesic from $I$ to $-I$ in $O(2m)$ has index $\ge 2m - 2$. For $A$ with blocks $a_j\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, $a_1 \ge \dots \ge a_m > 0$ odd, the non-zero eigenvalues of $K_A$ are $(a_i + a_j)^2/4$ for $i < j$ and $(a_i - a_j)^2/4$ for $i < j$ with $a_i \neq a_j$, each counted twice; so $\lambda = \sum_{i<j}(a_i + a_j - 2) + \sum_{a_i > a_j}(a_i - a_j - 2)$.

lean.statement: For integers $a_1, \dots, a_m$ put $\lambda(a) = \sum_{i < j}(a_i + a_j - 2) + \sum_{a_i > a_j}(a_i - a_j - 2)$, the second sum over ordered pairs. Let all $a_j$ be odd and positive. (i) The index, in the sense of Chapter 14 (V14.8), of the spectrum consisting of $\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(a_i + a_j)^2$ for $i < j$ and $\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(a_i - a_j)^2$ for $a_i > a_j$, each counted twice, is $\lambda(a)$. (ii) If all $a_j = 1$, $\lambda(a) = 0$. (iii) If not all $a_j = 1$, $\lambda(a) \ge 2m - 2$.

diff: Milnor's spectrum is taken as given: its computation, and Theorem 20.5 for $O(n)$, are not formalized. The index is the count of conjugate parameters of V14.8, for the velocity $\pi A$.
The bound for the geodesics themselves is V15.30, proved without the spectrum.

items.title: The spaces $\Omega_k(n)$

milnor.label: §24, p. 136
milnor.statement: With fixed anticommuting complex structures $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, $\Omega_k(n)$ is the set of all complex structures which anticommute with them. $\Omega_k(n) \subset \Omega_{k-1}(n) \subset \dots \subset \Omega_1(n) \subset O(n)$; "clearly each $\Omega_k(n)$ is a compact set"; $\Omega_0(n) = O(n)$.

lean.statement: $\Omega_0(n) = O(n)$, and for $k \ge 1$, $\Omega_k(n)$ is the set of complex structures $J$ with $J_\alpha J = -JJ_\alpha$ for $1 \le \alpha \le k - 1$. For any fixed matrices $J_\alpha$, $\Omega_{k+1}(n) \subseteq \Omega_k(n)$, and every $\Omega_k(n)$ is closed and compact. $J_1, \dots, J_k$ form an anticommuting family if each is a complex structure and $J_\alpha J_\beta = -J_\beta J_\alpha$ for $\alpha \neq \beta$; then $J_k \in \Omega_k(n)$ for $k \ge 1$.

diff: The inclusions and the compactness hold for any fixed matrices $J_\alpha$. An anticommuting family $J_1, \dots, J_k$ includes the base point $J_k \in \Omega_k(n)$.

items.title: Lemma 24.4: the reflection preserves $\Omega_k(n)$

milnor.label: §24, p. 136
milnor.statement: Each component of $\Omega_k(n)$ is a symmetric space: the isometric reflection of $O(n)$ in a point of $\Omega_k(n)$ automatically carries $\Omega_k(n)$ to itself.

lean.statement: For $k \ge 1$ and $P, J' \in \Omega_k(n)$, $-PJ'P \in \Omega_k(n)$. Since $J'^{-1} = -J'$ for a complex structure, $-PJ'P = PJ'^{-1}P$ is the image of $J'$ under $\sigma \mapsto P\sigma^{-1}P$, the reflection of $O(n)$ in $P$ (Lemma 21.1).

diff: Only $-PJ'P \in \Omega_k(n)$. That the reflection is an isometry and that the components are symmetric spaces are not formalized.

items.title: Assertions 1 and 2, the "if" halves

milnor.label: §24, Assertions 1 and 2, p. 137
milnor.statement: For small skew $A$: $J\exp A$ is a complex structure if and only if $A$ anticommutes with $J$ (Assertion 1); $J\exp A$ anticommutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ if and only if $A$ commutes with them (Assertion 2).

lean.statement: If $J$ is a complex structure and $A$ is skew with $AJ = -JA$, then $J\exp A$ is a complex structure. If $J_\alpha J = -JJ_\alpha$ and $A$ commutes with $J_\alpha$, then $J_\alpha$ anticommutes with $J\exp A$.

diff: The "if" halves need no smallness. The "only if" halves are V15.22.

items.title: From $\Omega_k(n)$ to $\Omega_{k+1}(n)$, algebraically; the Remark

milnor.label: §24, proof of Lemma 24.4 and Remark, pp. 137–138
milnor.statement: For $J_k \in \Omega_k(n)$ and a complex structure $J = J_kA$ anticommuting with $J_1, \dots, J_k$, $A$ is a complex structure which anticommutes with $J_k$ and commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$; so $t \mapsto J_k\exp(\pi tA)$ is a geodesic from $J_k$ to $-J_k$ in $\Omega_k(n)$; and conversely. Remark: $J_kA$ is the midpoint $\gamma(\tfrac12)$.

lean.statement: Let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ ($k \ge 1$) be an anticommuting family. (i) If $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$, then $A = -J_kJ'$ ($= J_k^{-1}J'$) is a complex structure that anticommutes with $J_k$ and commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$, and $J' = J_kA$. (ii) Conversely, for every such $A$, $J_kA \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$. (iii) For $J' \in \Omega_{k+1}(n)$ and every real $t$, $\cos t\,J_k + \sin t\,J' \in \Omega_k(n)$, and $J_k\exp(tA) = \cos t\,J_k + \sin t\,J'$ for $A = -J_kJ'$: the curve $t \mapsto J_k\exp(tA)$ stays in $\Omega_k(n)$, passes through $J'$ at $t = \pi/2$ and reaches $-J_k$ at $t = \pi$. (iv) A complex structure $J'$ anticommuting with a matrix $J$ satisfies $\operatorname{tr}(J'^{\mathsf T}J) = 0$.

diff: (iii) is about the curve $\cos t\,J_k + \sin t\,J'$ staying in $\Omega_k(n)$; that it is a minimal geodesic, and that all minimal geodesics arise so, are V15.25–V15.26.
(iv), the orthogonality of $J'$ and $J$ for the trace form, is not in the book.

items.title: Milnor's imbedding $\Omega_k(n) \to \Omega_k(n + n')$

milnor.label: §24, p. 138
milnor.statement: Choose fixed anticommuting complex structures $J'_1, \dots, J'_k$ on $\mathbb R^{n'}$. Then each $J \in \Omega_k(n)$ determines a complex structure $J \oplus J'_k$ on $\mathbb R^n \oplus \mathbb R^{n'}$ which anticommutes with $J_\alpha \oplus J'_\alpha$ for $\alpha = 1, \dots, k - 1$.

lean.statement: If $J_1, \dots, J_k$ and $J'_1, \dots, J'_k$ are anticommuting families on $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^{n'}$, the block matrices $J_\alpha \oplus J'_\alpha$ form an anticommuting family on $\mathbb R^n \oplus \mathbb R^{n'}$. For any fixed matrices and every $k$: if $P \in \Omega_k(n)$ for the $J_\alpha$ and $P' \in \Omega_k(n')$ for the $J'_\alpha$, then $P \oplus P' \in \Omega_k(n + n')$ for the $J_\alpha \oplus J'_\alpha$. With $P' = J'_k$ (V15.4) this is Milnor's map $J \mapsto J \oplus J'_k$.

diff: $\mathbb R^{n'}$ must carry $k$ anticommuting complex structures (V15.9 supplies them for $n' = 16r'$). The direct limit $\Omega_k$ is not formed; the compatibility with $\varphi$ is V15.41.

items.title: Explicit anticommuting complex structures

milnor.label: §24, pp. 136, 139
milnor.statement: "Assume that $n$ is divisible by a high power of $2$", and let $J_1, \dots, J_{k-1}$ be fixed complex structures which anticommute; later, $n = 16r$. The structures are never written down.

lean.statement: With $\sigma = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, $\tau = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, $\kappa = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$, explicit Kronecker products give one complex structure on $\mathbb R^2$ ($\sigma$), three anticommuting ones on $\mathbb R^4$ ($1 \otimes \sigma$, $\sigma \otimes \tau$, $\sigma \otimes \kappa$), seven on $\mathbb R^8$, and eight on $\mathbb R^{16}$ (the seven tensored with $\tau$, and $1 \otimes 1 \otimes 1 \otimes \sigma$). Renaming the coordinates and repeating block-diagonally ($J_\alpha \oplus \dots \oplus J_\alpha$) preserve anticommuting families; so $\mathbb R^{16r}$ carries eight anticommuting complex structures for every $r$.

diff: Explicit Kronecker products make the standing assumptions of §24 non-vacuous for $n = 16r$ and $k \le 8$.

items.title: Products of anticommuting complex structures

milnor.label: §24, pp. 139–143
milnor.statement: $J_1J_2J_3$ has square $+I$ and commutes with $J_1$ and $J_2$; $J_3J_4$ anticommutes with it; the corresponding statements for $J_1J_4J_5$, $J_2J_4J_6$, $J_1J_6J_7$ and $J_7J_8$; for $k = 7$, $J_7 = \pm J_1J_2J_3J_4J_5J_6$. Stated without computation.

lean.statement: In any ring, call $J_1, \dots, J_k$ Clifford if $J_\alpha^2 = -1$ and $J_\alpha J_\beta = -J_\beta J_\alpha$ for $\alpha \neq \beta$ ($1 \le \alpha, \beta \le k$); an anticommuting family of matrices is Clifford. Put $\theta_3 = J_1J_2J_3$, $\theta_5 = J_1J_4J_5$, $\theta_6 = J_2J_4J_6$, $\theta_7 = J_1J_6J_7$ and $\omega_7 = J_1J_2\cdots J_7$. Then, whenever $k$ is large enough for the indices involved: $\theta_3^2 = 1$, $\theta_3$ commutes with $J_1, J_2, J_3$ and anticommutes with $J_\alpha$ for $4 \le \alpha \le k$; $J_3J_4$ anticommutes with $\theta_3$ and commutes with $J_1, J_2$; $\theta_5^2 = 1$, $\theta_5$ commutes with $J_1, J_4, J_5, \theta_3$ and anticommutes with $J_2, J_3$; $\theta_6^2 = 1$, $\theta_6$ commutes with $J_2, J_4, J_6, \theta_3, \theta_5$ and anticommutes with $J_1, J_3, J_5$; $\theta_7^2 = 1$, $\theta_7$ commutes with $J_1, J_6, J_7, \theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6$ and anticommutes with $J_2, \dots, J_5$; $J_7J_8$ commutes with $\theta_3, \theta_5, \theta_6$ and anticommutes with $\theta_7$; $\omega_7 = -\theta_3\theta_5\theta_7$, and it commutes with $J_1, \dots, J_7$.

items.title: Lemma 24.6, the odd steps (3), (5), (6), (7)

milnor.label: §24, Lemma 24.6 (3), (5), (6), (7), pp. 139–141
milnor.statement: $\Omega_3(16r)$ is the quaternionic Grassmann manifold of $\mathbb H^{4r}$, through the $+1$-eigenspace $V_1$ of $J_1J_2J_3$; $\Omega_5(16r)$ the subspaces $W \subset V_1$ closed under $J_1$ with $V_1 = W \oplus J_2W$; $\Omega_6(16r)$ the real subspaces $X \subset W$ with $W = X \oplus J_1X$; $\Omega_7(16r)$ the real Grassmann manifold of $X \cong \mathbb R^{2r}$.

items.title: Lemma 24.6, the dimensions

milnor.label: §24, pp. 139–141
milnor.statement: The splittings $V_1 \oplus V_2$, $W \oplus J_2W$, $X \oplus J_1X$, $X_1 \oplus X_2$. Milnor restricts attention to the components with $\dim_{\mathbb H}V_1 = \dim_{\mathbb H}V_2 = 2r$ and with $\dim X_1 = \dim X_2 = r$.

lean.statement: On a finite-dimensional real vector space $V$, if $\theta^2 = 1$ and an injective $P$ anticommutes with $\theta$, then $\dim V = 2\dim\{\theta = 1\}$ ($P$ exchanges the $\pm1$-eigenspaces of $\theta$). Hence, for Clifford $J_1, \dots, J_8$ on $V$, with $V_1 = \{\theta_3 = 1\}$, $W = V_1 \cap \{\theta_5 = 1\}$, $X = W \cap \{\theta_6 = 1\}$ and $X_1 = X \cap \{\theta_7 = 1\}$: $\dim V = 2\dim V_1 = 4\dim W = 8\dim X = 16\dim X_1$, the halvings being effected by $J_4$, $J_2$, $J_1$ and $J_7J_8$. For $\mathbb R^{16r}$ with the structures of V15.9, $\dim V_1 = 8r$, $\dim W = 4r$, $\dim X = 2r$ and $\dim X_1 = r$.

items.title: Minimal spaces and the numbers $m_k$

milnor.label: §24, p. 143
milnor.statement: $V$ is a minimal $(J_1, \dots, J_k)$-space if no proper, non-trivial subspace is closed under the action of $J_1, \dots, J_k$. $m_k$ is the dimension of a minimal space: $m_0, \dots, m_8 = 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, 16$, and for $k > 8$ "it can be shown that $m_k = 16m_{k-8}$".

lean.statement: A real vector space $V$ with linear maps $J_1, J_2, \dots$ is minimal for $J_1, \dots, J_k$ if $V \neq 0$ and every subspace closed under $J_1, \dots, J_k$ is $0$ or $V$. The numbers $m_k$ are defined by the table $m_0, \dots, m_8 = 1, 2, 4, 4, 8, 8, 8, 8, 16$ and $m_{k+8} = 16m_k$.

items.title: $m_k$ divides the dimension, and is the least one

milnor.label: §24, p. 143
milnor.statement: The values $m_0, \dots, m_8$ are read off from the description of the minimal spaces: lines over $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, $\mathbb H$, then $H \oplus H'$, $L$, $L \oplus L'$. For $k > 8$ "it can be shown that $m_k = 16 m_{k-8}$", and the Remark that follows (pp. 143–144) takes a space of dimension $r m_k$, for any $k$.

lean.statement: On a real vector space: one $J$ with $J^2 = -1$ makes the dimension even ($V$ is a $\mathbb C$-module); two anticommuting ones make it divisible by $4$ ($V$ is an $\mathbb H$-module, through Mathlib's quaternion algebra); four Clifford maps on a finite-dimensional $V$ make it divisible by $8$; and for $k \le 8$, Clifford $J_1, \dots, J_k$ on a finite-dimensional $V$ force $m_k \mid \dim V$. items.title: The Clifford algebra

milnor.label: §24, footnote, p. 136
milnor.statement: These structures make $\mathbb R^n$ into a module over a suitable Clifford algebra; "the Clifford algebras will be suppressed in the following presentation".

lean.statement: Let $C_k$ be Mathlib's Clifford algebra of the quadratic form $Q(x) = -\sum x_i^2$ on $\mathbb R^k$. Clifford elements $J_1, \dots, J_k$ of a real algebra $A$ determine an algebra homomorphism $C_k \to A$ sending the $i$-th basis vector to $J_i$; $\dim C_k = 2^k$; and a minimal $(J_1, \dots, J_k)$-space has dimension at most $2^k$, being the image of $C_k$ under $c \mapsto c\cdot u$ for any $u \neq 0$.

diff: Clifford maps give a module over $C_k$, of dimension $2^k$; so a minimal space has dimension $\le 2^k$, the tool of V15.16.

items.title: Lemma 24.8: minimal spaces have dimension $m_k$

milnor.label: §24, p. 143
milnor.statement: A minimal space is a line over $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb C$, $\mathbb H$ for $k = 0, 1, 2$; a quaternionic line with $J_3 = \pm J_1J_2$ for $k = 3$; $H \oplus H'$ for $k = 4, 5, 6$; for $k = 7$, $J_7 = \pm J_1J_2J_3J_4J_5J_6$; $L \oplus L'$ for $k = 8$. The proof "follows that of 24.6".

lean.statement: Let $k \le 8$ and let $J_1, \dots, J_k$ be Clifford on a finite-dimensional real $V$. If $V$ is minimal, $\dim V = m_k$; conversely, if $\dim V = m_k$, $V$ is minimal; a minimal $V$ has $m_k \le \dim V \le 2^k$. An involution commuting with all $J_\alpha$ acts on a minimal space as $1$ or as $-1$; hence a minimal space for $k = 3$ (resp. $7$) is minimal for $J_1, J_2$ (resp. $J_1, \dots, J_6$), the involution being $J_1J_2J_3$ (resp. $J_1\cdots J_7$).

$J_1J_2J_3$ and $J_1\cdots J_7$ act as $\pm1$ on a minimal space because they are central involutions.

items.title: Lemma 24.8 (Bott and Shapiro): uniqueness

milnor.label: §24, Lemma 24.8
milnor.statement: For $k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, any two minimal $(J_1, \dots, J_k)$ vector spaces are isomorphic: there is an isometry between them which commutes with the action of $J_1, \dots, J_k$.

lean.statement: Let $k \le 8$ with $k \not\equiv 3 \pmod 4$, and let $V$, $V'$ be finite-dimensional real spaces with Clifford $J_1, \dots, J_k$ and $J'_1, \dots, J'_k$, both minimal. Then there is a linear isomorphism $T : V \to V'$ with $T(J_\alpha v) = J'_\alpha(Tv)$ for all $\alpha \le k$ and $v \in V$.

diff: A linear isomorphism commuting with the $J_\alpha$, for $k \le 8$; no inner product is used. The isometric form would follow by polar decomposition, which is not formalized.

items.title: Vector fields on spheres

milnor.label: §24, Remark, pp. 143–144
milnor.statement: For anticommuting $J_1, \dots, J_k$ on a space of dimension $rm_k$ and each unit vector $u$, the $k$ vectors $J_1u, \dots, J_ku$ are perpendicular to each other and to $u$: $k$ linearly independent vector fields on an $(rm_k - 1)$-sphere; $3$ on a $(4r - 1)$-sphere, $7$ on an $(8r - 1)$-sphere, $8$ on a $(16r - 1)$-sphere (Hurwitz and Radon; Adams: best possible).

lean.statement: If $J_1, \dots, J_k$ are anticommuting complex structures on $\mathbb R^n$, then for every $u$, $\langle J_\alpha u, J_\beta u\rangle = \delta_{\alpha\beta}|u|^2$ and $\langle J_\alpha u, u\rangle = 0$; so for $|u| = 1$ the $J_\alpha u$ are $k$ orthonormal vectors tangent to the unit sphere at $u$. This is written out for the eight structures of V15.9 on $\mathbb R^{16r}$ (eight fields on $S^{16r-1}$), and the general statement applies to the block-diagonal families on $\mathbb R^{4r}$ and $\mathbb R^{8r}$ built from V15.9 (three and seven fields).

diff: The orthonormality identities, written out for the eight structures on $\mathbb R^{16r}$. The general count and Adams's theorem are not formalized.

items.title: The index count for $k \not\equiv 2 \pmod 4$, from the spectrum

milnor.label: §24, Assertions, pp. 145–146
milnor.statement: $K_A$ has at least $s - 1$ eigenvalues which are $\ge (3 + 1)^2/4 = 4$. Each eigenvalue $e^2$ of $K_A$ gives rise to conjugate points for $t = e^{-1}, 2e^{-1}, 3e^{-1}, \dots$; hence the index of a non-minimal geodesic from $J$ to $-J$ in $\Omega_k(n)$ is $\ge n/m_{k+1} - 1$.

lean.statement: The index of a spectrum (in the sense of Chapter 14, V14.8) is at least the number of its eigenvalues greater than $\pi^2$. Hence, for integers $a_1, \dots, a_s \ge 1$ with some $a_{h_0} \ge 3$, the $s - 1$ eigenvalues $\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(a_{h_0} + a_j)^2$, $j \neq h_0$, already have index at least $s - 1$.

Oddness of the $a_j$ is not needed.

items.title: The index count for $k \equiv 2 \pmod 4$, from the spectrum

milnor.label: §24, pp. 147–148
milnor.statement: On a fixed component, $a_1, \dots, a_r$ are odd with sum $c$ and $\max|a_h| \ge 3$, and $2\lambda \ge \sum_{a_h > a_j}(a_h - a_j - 2)$. "Suppose for example that some $a_h$ is equal to $-3$": then $4\lambda \ge 2p \ge r + c$, where $r = n/m_k$.

lean.statement: Let $a_1, \dots, a_r$ be odd integers, some $|a_h| \ge 3$, and $c = \sum_h a_h$. Then $\sum_{a_h > a_j}(a_h - a_j - 2) \ge (r - |c|)/2$; equivalently, the index (V14.8) of the spectrum with one eigenvalue $\tfrac{\pi^2}{4}(a_h - a_j)^2$ for each pair $a_h > a_j$ is at least $(r - |c|)/4$.
